Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs

A compact cross-language safety kernel supplies shared FFN coordinates for mechanistic diagnosis and masked LoRA adaptation.

Xie Chengyu

October 17, 2026 ·Preprint ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

Safety Kernel identifies a compact set of safety-related neuron coordinates shared across languages. SCAR scores combine activation responsiveness and safety contrast on parallel safe and unsafe prompts; intersecting the language-wise candidate sets produces the kernel.

Suppression and activation-state transfer test its functional relevance. SK-Masked LoRA then restricts adaptation to the corresponding FFN output dimensions, linking the diagnosed shared mechanism to a specific parameter-update scope.

SCARLanguage-wise discovery score
Shared SKCross-language intersection
Masked LoRACoordinate-restricted adaptation

Cross-language alignment can be organized around a shared internal target whose behavior is tested before tuning.

Why this matters

External alignment supervision can improve multilingual safety without revealing which internal computation transfers the behavior. A common mechanistic target would help connect the languages used for discovery, the coordinates changed by training, and the languages used for evaluation.

How it works

  1. Compute language-wise SCAR scores from multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts.
  2. Intersect candidate neuron sets and test the kernel with suppression and activation-state transfer.
  3. Constrain LoRA adaptation to the selected FFN output dimensions and evaluate cross-language defense and capability retention.

What the study finds

The study combines compactness measurements, masking tests, and activation-state interventions across model backbones. Safety comparisons include languages excluded from kernel discovery, alongside analyses of selection scope, update scope, kernel composition, and general capabilities.

What this means

The framework creates a clearer chain from observation to control: identify a shared set, test what changing it does, and tune within its coordinates. This makes multilingual transfer more interpretable than a performance improvement considered without an internal account.

The kernel is defined by the discovery procedure and language set, rather than being an unconditional property of every model. Studying its composition and held-out transfer helps establish when a compact shared target is a useful basis for intervention.
